core.text: 2 Related Work

Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used as high-level planners and interactive controllers that map natural-language goals to action sequences. (Achiam et al., 2023; Touvron et al., 2023; Grattafiori et al., 2024) Prompting strategies such as Chain-of-Thought expose intermediate reasoning that can improve multi-step decision making. (Wei et al., 2022) ReAct couples reasoning traces with action/tool calls, enabling agents to iteratively ground information through interaction. (Yao et al., 2022) Reflexion and related trial-and-revision paradigms leverage feedback from failures to refine subsequent attempts. (Shinn et al., 2023) Despite strong empirical performance, LLM agents remain brittle when correctness depends on unobserved constraints or environment-specific dynamics that are not captured in the prompt. (Valmeekam et al., 2023; Kambhampati et al., 2024; Wang et al., 2024) More broadly, evaluations of LLM planning highlight systematic feasibility and constraint-satisfaction failures under realistic settings. (Valmeekam et al., 2023; Stein et al., 2023; Wu et al., 2025)

A parallel line of work reduces online interaction by predicting unobserved facts using learned world models. (Ha and Schmidhuber, 2018; Schrittwieser et al., 2020) In LLM-agent settings, world-model-centric approaches can lower interaction cost, but may fail silently when predicted preconditions are treated as truth. (Qiao et al., 2024; Wang et al., 2024) WKM exemplifies parametric prediction to support planning without explicit online verification of every missing predicate. (Qiao et al., 2024) Programmatic world modeling adds an executable substrate for simulation: WorldCoder induces code-level environment models and plans against the induced simulator. (Tang et al., 2024) However, correctness in programmatic simulation remains sensitive to mismatches between induced dynamics and the runtime environment, especially under distribution shift. (Tang et al., 2024; Wang et al., 2024) AEC is complementary: it treats world-model outputs as beliefs for pruning and gates commitment on grounded-only verification, so model errors primarily affect efficiency rather than feasibility. (Qiao et al., 2024; Tang et al., 2024)

Neurosymbolic agents increasingly incorporate induced rules or constraints to override unreliable predictions and enforce discovered environment regularities. (Zhou et al., 2024) WALL-E is a representative failure-driven refinement approach that learns override rules from counterexamples collected during interaction and iterates to improve performance. (Zhou et al., 2024) Such refinement loops are effective, but they still face the decision problem of which beliefs must be grounded before committing to a plan in a new episode. (Zhou et al., 2024; Kaelbling et al., 1998) AEC can reuse the same kind of trial feedback, but our emphasis is the control layer that arbitrates between querying (to ground facts) and simulating (to cheaply filter hypotheses) while maintaining a grounded-only commitment story. (Zhou et al., 2024; Kaelbling et al., 1998)

AEC is closely related to planning under partial observability, where an agent must trade off information acquisition cost against the risk of acting on incorrect beliefs. (Kaelbling et al., 1998; Albore et al., 2009) Classical POMDP and contingent-planning formulations provide principled treatments of epistemic actions, but exact solutions are often intractable and require accurate models. (Kaelbling et al., 1998; Albore et al., 2009) In contrast, many LLM-agent methods rely on implicit uncertainty (e.g., self-consistency) or ad hoc heuristics for verification decisions. (Wei et al., 2022; Yao et al., 2022; Kambhampati et al., 2024) AEC makes uncertainty operational as an explicit control signal (query vs. simulate) while preventing belief leakage by conditioning predictions only on grounded facts. (Kaelbling et al., 1998)

Symbolic planning provides formal guarantees when the domain model and state are correct, but typically requires substantial domain engineering and struggles with missing or noisy state. (Ghallab et al., 2004; Helmert, 2006) Recent neurosymbolic approaches introduce explicit verifiers or constraint checkers to filter candidate plans produced by neural components. (Valmeekam et al., 2023; Wang et al., 2024) AEC’s verifier combines grounded precondition coverage (via sound-but-incomplete entailment) with a categorical compatibility check inherited from SQ-BCP, so plan commitment depends only on grounded evidence. (Qu, 2026) This positions AEC as a lightweight safety gate that can sit atop LLM planners and learned world models without requiring predicted beliefs to be treated as truth. (Qu, 2026; Kaelbling et al., 1998)
3 Active Epistemic Control Framework
3.1 Background: Category-Theoretic Planning

We build on the categorical planning formalism introduced in SQ-BCP (Qu, 2026). A planning problem is represented as a category whose objects are world states and whose morphisms are actions (or action compositions). This perspective isolates (i) structural feasibility from (ii) the epistemic challenge induced by partial observability.

In our benchmarks, a world state is represented by a set of typed predicate facts. A candidate plan (hypothesis) hh is a composed morphism annotated with (a) a precondition set Pre⁡(h)\mathrm{Pre}(h) and (b) an expected binary assignment h.expected⁡(p)∈{0,1}h.\mathrm{expected}(p)\in\{0,1\} for each p∈Pre⁡(h)p\in\mathrm{Pre}(h) (as produced by the planner/annotator). AEC does not require a particular hypothesis generator: any procedure that outputs a finite set of candidates HH with Pre⁡(h)\mathrm{Pre}(h) and h.expected⁡(⋅)h.\mathrm{expected}(\cdot) is compatible.
3.2 Epistemic State: Grounded Facts vs. Beliefs
AEC maintains an explicit separation between grounded (externally supported) facts and beliefs (model predictions) used only for hypothesis pruning.

An epistemic state is a triple s=(w,w^,H)s=(w,\hat{w},H), where ww is a set of grounded predicate assignments, w^\hat{w} is a belief store of tuples (p,v^p,σp)(p,\hat{v}_{p},\sigma_{p}), and HH is a set of candidate hypotheses (plans).

ww contains only facts obtained from (i) the initial observation w0w_{0} (grounded but partial), and (ii) subsequent environment interactions that provide verifiable evidence (queries and/or execution feedback). Unobserved predicates are not assumed false; they remain unknown until grounded.

w^\hat{w} contains tentative predictions only and is never treated as truth. Each entry (p,v^p,σp)(p,\hat{v}_{p},\sigma_{p}) records a discretized belief v^p∈{0,1}\hat{v}_{p}\in\{0,1\} together with an epistemic uncertainty estimate σp∈[0,1]\sigma_{p}\in[0,1].

Let dom⁡(w)={p∣(p,v)∈w}\mathrm{dom}(w)=\{p\mid(p,v)\in w\} and dom⁡(w^)={p∣(p,v^,σ)∈w^}\mathrm{dom}(\hat{w})=\{p\mid(p,\hat{v},\sigma)\in\hat{w}\}. For any hypothesis hh, we write the unresolved set as
U⁡(w,w^,h)={p∈Pre⁡(h)∣p∉dom⁡(w)∪dom⁡(w^)}.U(w,\hat{w},h)=\{p\in\mathrm{Pre}(h)\mid p\notin\mathrm{dom}(w)\cup\mathrm{dom}(\hat{w})\}. (1)
AEC repeatedly selects p∈U⁡(⋅)p\in U(\cdot) to resolve until either all remaining candidates are verifiable or the query budget is exhausted.

All predictions are conditioned only on grounded facts ww, never on beliefs w^\hat{w}. This prevents self-confirming feedback loops in which earlier model guesses become inputs that reinforce later guesses.
3.3 Queries and Grounded Updates
AEC resolves unknown predicates via (i) external queries that ground facts, or (ii) world-model simulation that creates beliefs used only for hypothesis filtering.

A query Query​(p)\textsc{Query}(p) is a macro-action that verifies predicate pp through environment interaction (possibly multiple primitive steps), parses the resulting observation to obtain v∈{0,1}v\in\{0,1\}, and returns any additional grounded facts revealed after the query. Importantly, queries need not be reversible (e.g., opening a container changes the environment). Therefore, after querying pp we update the grounded store as
(v,Δ​w)←Query​(p)w←w∪{(p,v)}∪Δ​w.\begin{split}(v,\Delta w)&\leftarrow\textsc{Query}(p)\\ w&\leftarrow w\cup\{(p,v)\}\cup\Delta w.\end{split} (2)
This ensures ww remains a sound representation of all grounded facts available to the agent.
3.4 Predictive Model Interface and Ambiguity Margin
AEC requires a predictor that estimates both a belief score and epistemic uncertainty:
Mθ:(w,p)↦(μp,σp),M_{\theta}:(w,p)\mapsto(\mu_{p},\sigma_{p}), (3)
where μp∈[0,1]\mu_{p}\in[0,1] estimates whether predicate pp holds given grounded facts ww, and σp∈[0,1]\sigma_{p}\in[0,1] is an epistemic uncertainty estimate.

The AEC controller uses MθM_{\theta} only through (μp,σp)(\mu_{p},\sigma_{p}) and is otherwise agnostic to the specific uncertainty estimator (e.g., ensembles, Bayesian estimators). In practice, calibrated ensemble uncertainty provides a simple choice under partial observability. In our experiments, MθM_{\theta} follows the same LLM-based predictive interface used in WALL-E(Zhou et al., 2024) with ensemble output.
To avoid brittle switching near the decision boundary, AEC discretizes a prediction only when it is sufficiently far from 0.50.5:
v^p=𝟙[μp≥0.5]only if|μp−0.5|≥ϵ.\hat{v}_{p}=\mathbb{1}[\mu_{p}\geq 0.5]\quad\text{only if}\quad|\mu_{p}-0.5|\geq\epsilon. (4)
If |μp−0.5|<ϵ|\mu_{p}-0.5|<\epsilon, the prediction is treated as ambiguous and is resolved by querying.
3.5 Verification: Grounded Coverage + Categorical Consistency
AEC commits to a plan only if it passes a verifier that depends only on grounded facts (and sound entailment from them).
A verifier 𝒱⁡(h,w,w⋆)∈{True,False}\mathcal{V}(h,w,w^{\star})\in\{\textsc{True},\textsc{False}\} is sound if

𝒱⁡(h,w,w⋆)=True⇒{∀p∈Pre⁡(h):(p∈dom⁡(w))∨(w⊧p),Apply⁡(h,w)​satisfies goal constraints in​w⋆,\begin{split}&\mathcal{V}(h,w,w^{\star})=\textsc{True}\ \Rightarrow\ \\ &\begin{cases}\forall p\in\mathrm{Pre}(h):\big(p\in\mathrm{dom}(w)\big)\ \lor\ \big(w\models p\big),\\ \mathrm{Apply}(h,w)\ \text{satisfies goal constraints in}\ w^{\star},\end{cases}\end{split} (5)

where w⊧pw\models p denotes entailment via a fixed set of sound (but possibly incomplete) inference rules, and Apply⁡(h,w)\mathrm{Apply}(h,w) denotes symbolic execution of hh from ww (Definition 3.3).
Let hh be a composed morphism (plan) with action sequence (f1,…,fT)(f_{1},\dots,f_{T}). We define
Apply(h,w)=Eff(fT)∘⋯∘Eff(f1)(w),\mathrm{Apply}(h,w)\;=\;\mathrm{Eff}(f_{T})\circ\cdots\circ\mathrm{Eff}(f_{1})(w),
i.e., the symbolic state obtained by applying the effects of each action in sequence.
We implement 𝒱\mathcal{V} as the conjunction of: (i) a precondition coverage check (grounded-or-entailed), and (ii) a categorical pullback check (SQ-BCP) for compositional compatibility:
𝒱⁡(h,w,w⋆)=CheckPre​(h,w)∧PullbackVerify​(h,w,w⋆).\begin{split}\mathcal{V}(h,w,w^{\star})=&\textsc{CheckPre}(h,w)\ \land\ \\ &\textsc{PullbackVerify}(h,w,w^{\star}).\end{split} (6)

The entailment rules are sound but incomplete: they never assert false implications, but may fail to derive true ones, leading to additional queries or conservative rejections (efficiency loss only, not correctness).
3.6 Uncertainty-Guided Epistemic Control

Algorithm 1 presents the AEC policy. At each iteration, it selects a predicate p⋆∈Up^{\star}\in U, predicts (μ,σ)=Mθ​(w,p⋆)(\mu,\sigma)=M_{\theta}(w,p^{\star}) using grounded facts only, then either (i) queries (grounding p⋆p^{\star} and updating ww), or (ii) simulates (recording (p⋆,v^,σ)(p^{\star},\hat{v},\sigma) in w^\hat{w} and pruning HH). Finally, it commits to the best surviving hypothesis only if it passes verification on grounded facts.
3.7 Correctness: Simulation Affects Efficiency, Not Feasibility

AEC maintains a grounded store ww and a belief store w^\hat{w}. Querying may add facts to ww, while simulation adds entries only to w^\hat{w}. Crucially, plan commitment is gated by a verifier 𝒱\mathcal{V} that depends only on grounded facts ww (and not on w^\hat{w}). Therefore, simulation can affect which candidate plan survives, but cannot directly certify feasibility.
Consider one run of Algorithm 1. Let w0w_{0} be the initial grounded facts and let wfinalw_{\mathrm{final}} be the grounded facts at the moment a plan π\pi is committed. Define
Q:=dom⁡(wfinal)∖dom⁡(w0),Q\;:=\;\mathrm{dom}(w_{\mathrm{final}})\setminus\mathrm{dom}(w_{0}), (7)
i.e., the set of predicates whose truth values were grounded after initialization. Assume:

Grounded-only verification: π\pi is committed only if 𝒱⁡(π,wfinal,w⋆)=True\mathcal{V}(\pi,w_{\mathrm{final}},w^{\star})=\textsc{True}, and 𝒱\mathcal{V} depends only on wfinalw_{\mathrm{final}} (not on w^\hat{w}).
Verifier soundness: if all facts in wfinalw_{\mathrm{final}} are correct and 𝒱⁡(π,wfinal,w⋆)=True\mathcal{V}(\pi,w_{\mathrm{final}},w^{\star})=\textsc{True}, then π\pi is feasible.
Query error model: for each p∈Qp\in Q, the probability that the grounded value of pp in wfinalw_{\mathrm{final}} is incorrect is at most εoracle​(p)\varepsilon_{\mathrm{oracle}}(p).
Then the committed plan π\pi satisfies
Pr⁡(π​is feasible)≥ 1−∑p∈Qεoracle​(p).\Pr(\pi\ \text{is feasible})\;\geq\;1-\sum_{p\in Q}\varepsilon_{\mathrm{oracle}}(p). (8)
In particular, errors made by simulation-only predicates (those appearing only in w^\hat{w}) do not enter the bound.

Simulation never writes into ww, and the verifier reads only ww. Thus, if all facts in wfinalw_{\mathrm{final}} are correct, verifier soundness implies π\pi is feasible. The only facts in wfinalw_{\mathrm{final}} that can be incorrect are those grounded after initialization, namely predicates in QQ. By the query error model, each p∈Qp\in Q is incorrect with probability at most εoracle​(p)\varepsilon_{\mathrm{oracle}}(p). Therefore, by a union bound,
Pr⁡(∃p∈Q​s.t. p is incorrect)≤∑p∈Qεoracle​(p),\Pr(\exists\,p\in Q\ \text{s.t. $p$ is incorrect})\;\leq\;\sum_{p\in Q}\varepsilon_{\mathrm{oracle}}(p),
so with probability at least 1−∑p∈Qεoracle​(p)1-\sum_{p\in Q}\varepsilon_{\mathrm{oracle}}(p), all facts in wfinalw_{\mathrm{final}} are correct, and hence π\pi is feasible.

The guarantee above is per run: it relies only on grounded-only commitment and the query error model, and is independent of how the world model is trained. In our implementation, we optionally reuse success/failure trajectories across iterations to improve efficiency: counterexamples from failed episodes are aggregated to (i) update the backbone predictor or its calibration for precondition uncertainty, and (ii) patch verifier mismatches when a grounded query contradicts an entailed predicate. These updates change future query allocation and replanning frequency, but do not alter the fact that commitment in any given run is gated by 𝒱\mathcal{V} on grounded evidence.
4 Experiments

We evaluate Active Epistemic Control (AEC) on embodied planning tasks under partial observability. Our evaluation focus on (i) task completion, (ii) replanning behavior under failure, and (iii) LLM token usage. Our primary goal is to measure how grounded verification and uncertainty-guided querying affect success and replanning efficiency, without relying on iterative multi-episode training at test time.
4.1 Benchmarks

ALFWorld (Shridhar et al., 2020) is a household task benchmark in which an agent must complete language-conditioned goals (e.g., cool an apple then place it in the microwave) via discrete actions under partial observability. Episodes have a fixed interaction budget (50 steps in our setup). Many task-critical predicates (object locations, container states, object attributes such as clean/hot/cool) are not fully observable initially and must be resolved through interaction. Following prior work, we evaluate on the standard set of 134 predefined test tasks.

ScienceWorld (Wang et al., 2022) is an interactive science reasoning environment from AllenAI featuring long-horizon tasks (e.g., conducting experiments, manipulating objects, controlling environment conditions) under partial observability. ScienceWorld includes richer state transitions and more complex preconditions (e.g., temperature, phase changes, containment, device operation), making it a suitable stress test for AEC’s separation of grounded facts and beliefs as well as its verifier-based commitment rule. We will report results on a held-out test set following a standard train/test split used in prior ScienceWorld agent evaluations; details will be finalized with the released evaluation protocol and provided in the camera-ready version.
4.2 Evaluation Metrics
We report the following metrics
The percentage of tasks completed successfully within the episode budget.

The number of times the agent re-enters a planning phase for the same task due to execution failure or contradiction (e.g., an action fails, a queried predicate contradicts a plan precondition, or the verifier rejects the current best hypothesis). If the task is not completed, replanning rounds are set to a maximal cap.
4.3 Baselines
We compare against representative LLM-based planning and world-modeling approaches. All methods are evaluated with the same environment API and observation interface.
Direct: A direct LLM planner that proposes a plan from the task description and current observation, without explicit grounded verification.
ReAct (Yao et al., 2022): Interleaves reasoning and acting; replanning occurs naturally through interaction loops.
WKM (Qiao et al., 2024): A world-knowledge model that predicts missing state predicates without explicit grounded verification.
WALL-E (Zhou et al., 2024): Failure-driven refinement via learned neurosymbolic rules and MPC-style monitoring. We report results using the released codebase under the same evaluation caps as AEC.
Query-Only: An upper-bound variant that resolves all missing predicates through queries before committing to a plan (interaction- and token-heavy, but intended to reduce state uncertainty).
4.4 AEC Configuration

AEC requires a finite set of candidate plans HH. We generate a small set of diverse hypotheses from the initial grounded facts w0w_{0} and goal constraints w⋆w^{\star} using a single LLM planner. Each hypothesis includes an extracted precondition set Pre⁡(h)\mathrm{Pre}(h) and expected binary assignments h.expected⁡(p)h.\mathrm{expected}(p).

AEC uses a predictive model MθM_{\theta} that maps (w,p)(w,p) to a belief score μp\mu_{p} and uncertainty σp\sigma_{p}. The controller conditions only on grounded facts ww (no belief leakage), and discretizes predictions using an ambiguity margin ϵ\epsilon (Section 3). We use wall-E@5 as the world model

AEC queries predicates that are either ambiguous (|μp−0.5|<ϵ|\mu_{p}-0.5|<\epsilon) or high-uncertainty (σp>τ\sigma_{p}>\tau). We use a fixed ϵ\epsilon across all experiments and select τ\tau on a validation set.

AEC commits to a plan only if it passes a grounded verifier 𝒱\mathcal{V} consisting of (i) a precondition coverage check using grounded facts and sound entailment and (ii) a pullback-based compositional consistency check (Section 3).

Table 1 reports success rates on the 134 ALFWorld test tasks. Overall, AEC performs comparably to the strongest prior agents. AEC achieves 98.7% average success, which is close to WALL-E2.0 (98.3%) and above earlier LLM baselines such as WALL-E/RAFA (95%). We view this as evidence that the proposed epistemic control and grounded-only commitment can reduce a small number of residual failures even in a saturated regime.

While the absolute gains are modest, AEC attains robust performance across categories without relying on additional environment-specific metrics, supporting the claim that separating grounded facts from beliefs and gating commitment with verification is a reliable design choice for embodied planning under partial observability.

Table 2 reports results on ScienceWorld. We follow the WKM and split into Seen and Unseen tasks. AEC achieves 61.36 on Seen and 58.62 on Unseen, outperforming prior agents in Table 2. The gains are larger on Unseen (+3.87 over WKM), suggesting that AEC’s grounded-first epistemic control improves robustness when the environment distribution shifts. The result shows that AEC’s separation of grounded facts from model beliefs and verifier-gated commitment provides a general mechanism for mitigating compounding state-inference errors in partially observed, multi-step tasks.
5.3 Ablation Study
5.3.1 Components

To isolate the contributions of AEC components, we ablate two core mechanisms of AEC: (i) the verifier (“w/o verification” removes 𝒱\mathcal{V} and commits based on model-filtered hypotheses only), and (ii) the epistemic gating policy (“w/o gating” disables the uncertainty/ambiguity-based gating used to decide when to query vs. simulate, while keeping the rest of the pipeline unchanged).

Figure 1 summarizes the ablation on ALFWorld. The full AEC achieves a low failure rate (2) and requires fewer replanning rounds (3). Removing verification substantially degrades robustness: failure rate increases to 9 and replanning rises to 6, indicating that model-based hypothesis filtering alone is insufficient to reliably prevent infeasible commitments. Disabling gating yields a milder but consistent regression (failure rate 4; replanning 5), suggesting that uncertainty/ambiguity gating primarily stabilizes execution by avoiding overconfident simulation and reducing downstream plan revision.

We further evaluate AEC under different LLM backbones while keeping the overall pipeline (hypothesis generation, gating, and grounded verification) unchanged. Figure 2 shows that AEC remains effective across backbones: GPT-4 and Qwen3-14B achieve the highest success (98%), DeepSeek-R1-14B is slightly lower (97%), and Llama-3-8B exhibits a larger drop (91%). Overall, these results suggest that AEC’s gains are not tied to a single proprietary model; however, stronger backbones still translate into higher success, consistent with the role of the LLM planner/world model in generating and filtering candidate hypotheses.
5.3.2 Number of iterations.

Figure 3 shows the effect of running AEC with failure-driven refinement across iterations. Success increases from 88%88\% at iteration 0 to ≈98%\approx 98\% by iterations 3–4, with most gains realized in the first two iterations. This indicates that the dominant failure modes are corrected early, and further iterations provide diminishing returns. We attribute the improvement to the refinement procedure described in Section 3.
6 Conclusion

We presented Active Epistemic Control (AEC), a planning framework for partially observable environments that explicitly separates grounded facts from model beliefs. AEC uses a predictive world model to cheaply prune candidate hypotheses, but commits to a plan only through a verifier that depends solely on grounded evidence (with sound-but-incomplete entailment and categorical consistency checks). This design yields a clear separation of concerns: simulation improves efficiency by guiding which predicates to resolve, while feasibility is protected by grounded-only verification. Empirically, AEC achieves strong performance on ALFWorld and shows consistent gains over representative LLM-agent baselines, while remaining compatible with failure-driven refinement across iterations.

AEC’s guarantees are mediated by the grounding and verification interfaces: if the observation grounder or query oracle exhibits systematic errors (e.g., consistent visual misreads), AEC may incur conservative failures, extra replanning, or increased token cost even when a feasible plan exists. Moreover, our entailment rules are intentionally incomplete, which can inflate the set of unresolved predicates and shift work from logical inference to querying. Finally, AEC currently treats verification, replanning, and token usage as loosely coupled knobs rather than a single optimized objective.

These limitations suggest several directions. First, strengthen the verifier/grounder via counterexample-driven repair, including automatically detecting contradiction patterns and refining entailment rules or calibration thresholds from failure traces. Second, incorporate tighter decision objectives that jointly account for success, replanning rounds, and token usage, potentially learning instance-adaptive query thresholds rather than a fixed τ\tau. Third, evaluate broader generalization across environments with different observability and action semantics and characterize when improvements arise from better uncertainty estimation versus better hypothesis generation.
